tagline: The Caribbean's billionaire corridor — where St-Barths has no jet airport and the only smooth arrival is by sea.
summary: St-Maarten/St-Martin is the multi-flag (Dutch + French) air and yachting hub of the northeastern Caribbean, and its glamorous neighbour St-Barthélemy has one of the most famous short, steep airstrips in the world — no jets, weight-limited props only. The result is structural premium-transfer demand: visitors and homeowners reach St-Barths today by a small turboprop or a notoriously bouncy ferry across ~15 nm of open water. Add Anguilla (~8 nm) and the St Kitts & Nevis Leewards within Pioneer II range, and this is the densest billionaire-and-yacht cluster per nautical mile in the hemisphere.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Pioneer II owns the glamour corridor: St-Maarten↔St-Barths (~15 nm), ↔Anguilla (~8 nm), the St Kitts↔Nevis Narrows (~3 nm), and the Pioneer-edge run to St Kitts (~45 nm).
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR (H2 2026+) extends to Antigua (~60 nm) and across the Anegada Passage to the BVI (~80 nm), knitting the northern Leewards to the wider eastern-Caribbean network.

competitive_landscape: SXM↔St-Barths ferries (Voyager, Great Bay Express), Anguilla ferries, and weight-limited prop air (St-Barth Commuter, Winair) serve the cluster today — all demand proof and partners. Helicopters are the premium air analog. There is no foiling incumbent; the opportunity is comfort, quiet, and reliability for an extremely demanding clientele.
seasonality: Atlantic hurricane season (Jun–Nov, peak Sep) is the constraint (St-Maarten was hit hard by Irma in 2017); the glamour high season is Dec–Apr. The open channels (especially SXM↔SBH and the Anegada Passage) are where Navier's stabilized ride most differentiates.
regulatory_note: Multi-flag complexity is real: Dutch Kingdom (St-Maarten), France/EU (St-Barths & St-Martin), UK (Anguilla), and independent St Kitts & Nevis — each with its own maritime authority and customs. A premium operator that pre-clears across flags turns friction into a selling point. EU clean-maritime norms favor zero-emission operation on the French side.
